posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md: One thing I'm keen to see is how these perform over time. Are they intended to be one-use sensors or something that can be used over and over? If the latter, it seems to me that they'll degrade over time as the gelatin is regularly polluted by the solution it's immersed in unless measures are taken to prevent that. Thorough rinsing in distilled water after each use?

posts.author: Cab
posts.content_md:
> **MichaelH:** One thing I'm keen to see is how these perform over time. Are they intended to be one-use sensors or something that can be used over and over? If the latter, it seems to me that they'll degrade over time as the gelatin is regularly polluted by the solution it's immersed in unless measures are taken to prevent that. Thorough rinsing in distilled water after each use?

This all depends on what kind of polymer we're using; not all of our holograms are made in gelatin, in fact, most of them aren't. We use a range of gels, including polyacrylamide, poly hema, and various others that are essentially non degradable. Some of them we've autoclaved, some we've fed to active microbial cultures, and they keep coming back. I've got some holograms that I've used in experiments over, and over, and over again and they're as good now as they were when I made them. 

The complex part of this work lies getting a gel that gives a response to a specific analyte; if you want more information on that then a good place to start is with the website of the company through which this company is being exploited, Smart Holograms:

[http://www.smartholograms.com/site/sections/default.asp](http://www.smartholograms.com/site/sections/default.asp)

The gelatin ones will degrade if they're kept in a medium in which microbial action can take place; Rogers web site (the one linked to above) gives a good example of one in which that isn't an issue (in a whisky bottle). Gelatin is a marvellous material for making bright, pretty holograms, but it's perhaps more difficult to engineer into a smart gel for our type of work.

With regards to gelatin layers, around 1985 Ilford used to have a unique silver halide emulsion (SP-673). Exposed "under" water and developed with pyro, it could be kept for several months in a glycerol/water mixture. No fungus formed.

By the way, I still have some unexposed film sheets...

There are several obvious ways I can think of that can slow down the degradation of a gelatin film, but I'm trying to fit the whole glycerol/water thing in. I guess that at a sufficient concentration glycerol will slow down protease action, and it's a bacteriostatic. So my first inclination is that the product was merely a hard gelatin film, in itself slower to degrade, that was preserved with the glycerol.

There must have been some additional mechanism behind that particular film since none of all the other emulsions (from Agfa, Kodak, Slavich, HRT and even Ilford's HOTEC which was introduced to replace SP-673) did show any similar behavior.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md: I'm curious about something. Do the Smart Holograms detect the absolute quantity of a particular substance or the relative concentration? In other words, if the Smart Hologram were set to detect a substance and this substance were in solution which was gradually getting more and more concentrated, by say evaporation. Would the substance be detected at any concentration, or would it "turn on" at a specific concentration? This would be of immense benfit to DCG holographers who could easily determine the varying concentrations of an alcohol bath as the number of plates being processed increased, or the increase in concentration by evaporation of the alcohol when left overnight. I imagine it would be pretty useful for brewing as well. No more bulky glass tubes to determine specific gravity. When the Smart Hologram changes color, the beer's ready!

I am not familiar with the details of the polyHEMA alcohol sensor. I do know however, the relative alcohol concentration could be monitored by the wavelength shift of a reflection hologram system - maybe a la Walker/Benton. Of course any reflection hologram can be color shifted by putting a hologram in a solution of various amounts of alcohol (and water). I said "Walker/Benton" because some holographic emulsions (maybe due to their initial hardening) are likely to show a very non-linear behavior with respect to swelling. Walker/Benton advocated enzyme (trypsin) pre-treatment to get a more linear response.

posts.content_md:
> **Dinesh:** I'm curious about something. Do the Smart Holograms detect the absolute quantity of a particular substance or the relative concentration? In other words, if the Smart Hologram were set to detect a substance and this substance were in solution which was gradually getting more and more concentrated, by say evaporation. Would the substance be detected at any concentration, or would it "turn on" at a specific concentration?

That depends on what it's a hologram sensitive to; typically, they're sensitive over a range of concentrations (say, a continual colour change over a couple of pH units or over a concentration range of an ion). We can certainly put an alcohol sensor in a methanol/water mix and follow the change as the alcohol evaporates out.

> This would be of immense benfit to DCG holographers who could easily determine the varying concentrations of an alcohol bath as the number of plates being processed increased, or the increase in concentration by evaporation of the alcohol when left overnight. I imagine it would be pretty useful for brewing as well. No more bulky glass tubes to determine specific gravity. When the Smart Hologram changes color, the beer's ready!

The alcohol sensor is a really simple one; the ones we've give a continual colour change over a range of pH units. We've got some embodiments of the technology that, regrettably, I can't talk about right now which do just what you're asking; what we're in the process of doing right now is taking that technology and getting it put into real instruments. It's my hope that you'll be able to stick one on a bit of glassware and it'll tell you all about what's happening in the liquid mix; we've got a range of sensor holograms that'll do that, and we're in negotiations to see who there is out there who can make best use of them. I might have mentioned already somewhere here that I've used one of our alcohol sensors to follow ethanol production by yeast, and we've done the same with lactate being produced by lactobacillus (you can monitor all manner of microbial and food processes) but they're only some of our potential applications. For more info, have a look at the Smart Holograms web site.

posts.author: Cab
posts.content_md:
> **Martin:** I am not familiar with the details of the polyHEMA alcohol sensor. I do know however, the relative alcohol concentration could be monitored by the wavelength shift of a reflection hologram system - maybe a la Walker/Benton. Of course any reflection hologram can be color shifted by putting a hologram in a solution of various amounts of alcohol (and water). I said "Walker/Benton" because some holographic emulsions (maybe due to their initial hardening) are likely to show a very non-linear behavior with respect to swelling. Walker/Benton advocated enzyme (trypsin) pre-treatment to get a more linear response.

Getting the cross linking density right is a crucial part in the development of any of our sensors. Make it too soft and it goes shooting off out of the useful wavelength range, make it too hard and nothing happens; somewhere inbetween the two there's normally a range that gives us a linear response in the range of analyte concentrations we need.
